text.p: Tough, blunt-spoken Janet Reno, whom President Bill Clinton has decided to retain as his attorney general, has an independent streak that often upset the White House.

Reno, 58, whose future had been in doubt until Thursday night, faced White House complaints she was not a "team player" and sought too many special prosecutors to investigate the Whitewater affair involving the Clintons and other cases.
But the former Florida prosecutor insisted her decisions were based on the evidence and the law and said no one at the White House had ever told her of any unhappiness with her.
Clinton announced on Friday she would remain in his Cabinet.

Reno's defining moment as attorney general came when she was just 38 days in office. On April 19, 1993, she approved the disastrous raid by federal agents on the Branch Davidian cult's compound near Waco, Texas, to end a 51-day standoff.

Reno, who in 1993 was Clinton's third choice to serve as the nation's top law enforcement officer after two preferences ran into trouble, approved the ill-fated FBI raid after negotiations with cult leader David Koresh reached an impasse.
The armoured, tear-gas assault on the heavily armed cultists ended in an inferno that engulfed the compound, killing Koresh and about 80 followers and raising questions about Reno's judgment.
"I made the decision. I'm accountable. The buck stops with me," a grim-looking Reno said at a Justice Department news conference after the compound had burned to the ground.

The government charged Koresh's followers set the fire, while surviving cult members said it began when federal tanks knocked over lanterns as they battered down walls. Reno won widespread praise at first for taking responsibility but then many questions surfaced about her handling of the incident.
In her first year in office, she also saw morale plunge at the Justice Department because of personnel problems, poor relations with the White House and her brusque style.

Many of the problems started to disappear when Jamie Gorelick was brought in from the Pentagon in 1994 to become deputy attorney general in charge of running the Justice Department. With Gorelick in place, Reno could use her office as a bully pulpit, preaching about pet projects such as the need to reduce violence among young people and on television.

Reno got credit for a decisive performance after the truck bomb attack of April 19, 1995, on the Oklahoma City federal building, which killed 168 people. Appearing at the White House with Clinton seven hours after the blast, a determined Reno vowed to seek the death penalty for the perpetrators.
Reno, who is single, puts in long hours, often working weekends and living right across the street from the Justice Department. She takes few vacations.

Health problems arose in November 1995 when she revealed she suffered from Parkinson's disease, a degenerative illness that causes trembling and muscular rigidity. With typical spunk, Reno vowed to remain on the job.
The daughter of two Miami newspaper reporters, Reno received a chemistry degree from Cornell University in 1960 and then graduated from Harvard Law School three years later.
She began her career as a Miami lawyer and became the Dade County prosecutor in 1978, a post she held until Clinton named her as the first female U.S. attorney general.
